domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: Fabricated (hallucinated) references are entering the peer-reviewed literature faster than editors, reviewers and readers can verify them
affected_user: Journal editors and managing editors, peer reviewers, systematic reviewers and any researcher who builds on a reference list; secondarily research-integrity offices at publishers
job_to_be_done: Confirm that every reference in a submitted or published paper actually exists and says what the citing paper claims, before relying on it or publishing it
current_process: Reviewers spot-check a few references by hand; most journals do not run automated existence checks on reference lists at submission; readers assume references are real; integrity sleuths and Retraction Watch catch cases after publication
what_fails: Papers with non-existent references pass 3-5 expert reviewers (NeurIPS 2025 case) and get indexed; very few are corrected or retracted (one analysis found 2 of 619 affected papers retracted); the rate has risen sharply since mid-2024, coinciding with LLM writing tools
failure_frequency: An analysis reported by Retraction Watch (2026-05-07) found roughly 1 in 277 PubMed-indexed papers in 2026 contains at least one fabricated reference; a separate study of physics/chemistry/engineering/CS papers found 1 in 435 in early 2026, up from 1 in 1,600 in 2023; a Lancet audit of ~2.5M biomedical papers found ~3,000 papers with nonexistent references (12-fold rise since 2023). Figures differ across outlets.
cost_of_failure: unknown in dollars; qualitative cost is contaminated evidence base, wasted reader time chasing phantom sources, and retraction/correction workload for publishers. Former JAMA editors argue any paper with a hallucinated reference should be retracted.
existing_workaround: Manual DOI lookups by reviewers; ad hoc scripts against Crossref/OpenAlex; a sudden wave of open-source BibTeX checkers (citegate, bibverify, co-researcher) in 2026; some publishers piloting automated reference verification at submission as recommended by the Lancet authors
who_pays_today: Publishers (editorial staff time, integrity teams, retraction processing), reviewers (unpaid time), institutions investigating misconduct; vendors like Crossref/OpenAlex provide free APIs but no end-to-end check for most journals

sources.note: Reports an analysis finding 1 in 277 PubMed-indexed 2026 papers contain fabricated references; sharpest rise mid-2024.
Press coverage of the Lancet audit (~3,000 papers, 12-fold rise since 2023) and the call for automated reference verification at submission.
Secondary coverage of a study finding 1 in 435 early-2026 papers in physical sciences/CS with a fabricated reference and only 2 of 619 affected papers retracted.
Preprint surfaced in search on hallucinated citations evading NeurIPS 2025 review by 3-5 reviewers per paper; content not independently read.
235 public repos tagged citation-verification, most created/updated in 2026 (citegate 102 stars, bibverify 98, opendraft 523), showing a rush of DIY checkers.

firsthand_evidence: No individual firsthand reviewer complaint was captured (search budget exhausted). Closest signal: former JAMA editors publicly arguing that any paper with a hallucinated reference should be retracted, and Lancet authors asking publishers to add automated reference verification before peer review.
key_unknowns: Which journals already run automated checks; whether publishers will pay for a third-party service vs. build in-house (Crossref/OpenAlex APIs are free); how much reviewer time is actually spent on citation checking; whether the 1-in-277 figure holds across fields.
technical_unlock: Free scholarly metadata APIs (Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, arXiv) plus cheap LLM extraction of reference lists from PDFs make existence-and-claim checking feasible for a single developer; GitHub Actions-style CI gating of BibTeX (citegate) shows the pattern.
why_now: LLM writing tools drove a measurable jump in fabricated references from mid-2024; by May 2026 multiple large-scale audits were published and Retraction Watch/Forbes coverage put publishers under pressure; dozens of open-source checkers appeared in 2026.
existing_solutions: Open-source: citegate, bibverify, co-researcher, opendraft, CiteProof-AI-MCP; commercial integrity tools from publishers (e.g., STM Integrity Hub style screening, Clear Skies/Papermill Alarm were not confirmed in this search); Crossref/OpenAlex APIs. The DIY tool space is already crowded; the gap is adoption inside editorial workflows, not the check itself.

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: 2026 federal grant-making slowdown leaves PIs unable to learn the status of proposals or plan lab staffing
affected_user: US principal investigators (especially early-career), postdocs and grad students funded by NSF/NIH awards; university research offices providing bridge funding
job_to_be_done: Know whether and when a submitted proposal will be funded so the lab can hire, retain staff, buy instruments and commit to students
current_process: PIs submit via Research.gov/eRA Commons, then wait for program officer contact; status updates are informal (emails to program officers, rumor, trackers like Grant Witness); universities issue bridge funds case by case
what_fails: NSF awarded only ~613 grants by spring FY2026, about 20% of the FY2021-2024 pace; grant-making paused entirely June 4-12, 2026 and essentially flatlined after Aug 10; by Sept 2026 NSF was reported over $1B behind; the Major Research Instrumentation program suspended FY2026 applications and as of ~Oct 20, 2026 still had not opened its announced Oct 15-Nov 16 window; OMB apportionment review is slowing release of funds; Johns Hopkins reported a 28% decline in active award count; mid-cycle terminations and non-renewals are driving layoffs
failure_frequency: Systemic through FY2026; NSF awards at ~20% of normal pace (Grant Witness, spring 2026) and >$1B behind (Inside Higher Ed, 2026-09-21)
cost_of_failure: Lab closures, layoffs and lost student positions; UC Davis research office published guidance on the slowdown for faculty; Johns Hopkins 28% decline in active awards (CASRAI, summer 2026). Dollar totals per lab unknown.
existing_workaround: University bridge funding; PIs emailing program officers; Grant Witness and similar volunteer trackers compiling award data; labs shrinking headcount; applying to foundations
who_pays_today: Universities (bridge funds, research-admin staff time), PIs (unpaid uncertainty, lost personnel), advocacy groups funding trackers like Grant Witness

sources.note: Reports NSF MRI program silent on its announced Oct 15-Nov 16, 2026 submission window; NSF spokesperson says it is 'currently working to update this funding opportunity'.
Tracker documenting no NSF awards June 4-12, 2026 and calling the halts unprecedented.
NSF had awarded ~613 grants in FY2026, about 20% of the pace of FY2021-2024, per Grant Witness.
NSF over $1B behind on grants; awards flatlined since ~Aug 10, 2026.
Attributes part of slowdown to OMB using the apportionment process to slow release of funds.
University research office guidance to faculty on coping with the slowdown.
Attributes 2026 university layoffs to terminated/non-renewed NIH and NSF awards; cites Johns Hopkins 28% decline in active award count.
First Circuit upheld the block on the NIH 15% indirect-cost cap in Jan 2026; the cap is not in effect, so layoffs stem from terminations/delays rather than the cap.

firsthand_evidence: Scientific American reports scientists describing themselves as left in the dark about NSF application timelines, with the MRI program not even confirming when submissions will open (paraphrased).
key_unknowns: Whether the slowdown continues into FY2027; how many labs have actually closed; whether PIs would pay for status-tracking or planning tools, or whether this is purely a political problem with no product-shaped fix.
technical_unlock: Public award databases (NSF award API, NIH RePORTER) allow near-real-time tracking of award velocity by directorate and program; Grant Witness already does this. A solo developer could build program-level alerting, but cannot fix the underlying funding problem.
why_now: FY2026 is the first year with sustained, multi-month halts in NSF grant-making and an unresolved cap/budget fight; the FY2027 request again proposes a 15% indirect cap.
existing_solutions: Grant Witness (volunteer tracker), university research-office bulletins, pipeworx-io/mcp-nsf-awards (GitHub, free NSF award DB access), commercial pre-award tools (Cayuse, InfoReady) that do not address federal-side delay

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: Small academic labs track biological samples in spreadsheets, and irreplaceable samples are lost when freezers fail or people leave
affected_user: Grad students, postdocs and lab managers in small-to-mid academic wet labs (biology, biomedical); biobank-adjacent core labs
job_to_be_done: Know what is in every freezer box, who made it, when, and where it is, so samples can be found, reused, and recovered after a freezer or personnel event
current_process: Excel/Google Sheets box maps, handwritten labels, tribal knowledge; some labs use the free LabArchives freezer widget (described by a UW-Madison panel as not a true inventory) or paid tools (FreezerWorks ~$6K/yr license per the 2022 UW-Madison panel; DrFreezr listed at up to $400/mo)
what_fails: Unlabeled or unidentifiable tubes accumulate (University of Iowa EHS advises purging them); when a student leaves, nobody knows what tubes contain; when a -80C fails, labs cannot tell what was lost. High-profile cases: 147 McLean Hospital brain tissue samples lost to a freezer failure (Harvard Medical School news); a lawsuit alleging a custodian switched off a -80C freezer destroying years of research (NBC News, 2023).
failure_frequency: unknown; freezer-failure losses are episodic but institution-wide inventory programs (UW-Madison freezer panels 2018 and 2022, campus 'freezer challenges') indicate chronic rather than rare pain
cost_of_failure: Irreplaceable samples (Glasgow guidance notes some research samples are irreplaceable); the NBC-reported lawsuit concerned research described as taking years; commercial inventory licenses cost ~$6K/yr (FreezerWorks, 2022 figure) which small labs decline to pay
existing_workaround: Spreadsheets, paper box maps, periodic lab-wide freezer cleanouts, free LabArchives widget, Quartzy, and a steady stream of tiny home-grown open-source trackers (bioliams, aurora, drosodb, barcodex, labflow-eln: all 0-2 stars, all updated in 2026)
who_pays_today: Labs with budgets pay FreezerWorks/FreezerPro/eLabInventory; most small labs pay in grad-student time; institutions pay for freezer-challenge programs and EHS guidance

sources.note: UW-Madison lab-manager panel comparing Google Sheets, LabArchives widget (not a true inventory) and FreezerWorks (~$6K/yr).
Earlier campus discussion of freezer sample inventory practices; shows the problem is long-standing.
Lists DrFreezr freezer inventory tool at up to $400/month.
Loss of 147 brain tissue samples at McLean attributed to freezer digital controls.
Lawsuit over research lost when a custodian turned off a lab freezer.
University EHS recommends purging unidentifiable items and keeping a simple spreadsheet inventory.
Nine small open-source sample/freezer trackers, most 0-2 stars and updated in 2026, indicating repeated DIY attempts.

firsthand_evidence: No r/labrats thread was retrieved (search returned vendor and university pages only; budget then exhausted). Firsthand-adjacent: a UW-Madison panelist presented a Google Sheets freezer inventory as their lab's working solution.
key_unknowns: Current (2026) price points of FreezerWorks/eLabInventory/Quartzy; what fraction of small labs use spreadsheets vs. tools; whether PIs will pay $20-50/month from discretionary funds; how much Quartzy's free tier already covers.
technical_unlock: Phone-camera barcode/QR scanning, cheap label printers, and Supabase-style multi-tenant apps make a $0-30/month per-lab inventory feasible; LLM parsing of legacy spreadsheets could cut migration cost, which is the main adoption barrier.
why_now: Funding cuts (SCI-02) make $6K/yr licenses less affordable while lab turnover increases; several new open-source trackers appeared in 2026, signalling unmet demand.
existing_solutions: FreezerWorks, FreezerPro, Quartzy, eLabInventory/eLabFTW database module, LabArchives freezer widget, Benchling inventory, DrFreezr; open-source bioliams, aurora, MISO/SENAITE for larger facilities

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: Electronic lab notebook adoption stalls in academic labs, so protocols and results stay in paper notebooks that leave with the student
affected_user: PIs and grad students/postdocs in academic and government research labs; lab managers responsible for records when trainees leave
job_to_be_done: Record experiments so that a successor can reproduce a protocol and locate results years later, with minimal friction at the bench
current_process: Most academic and government labs still use paper notebooks (per a PMC-indexed review); hybrid workflows where undergrads write on paper and upload scans to a shared drive; some campuses (UW-Madison) mandate a campus ELN after pilots
what_fails: Adoption requires whole-department buy-in (most-cited barrier in a 169-respondent survey reported in search synthesis); bench-side note-taking is easier on paper and computers are impractical or unsafe at the bench; trainees resist; when a student leaves, protocol details are lost and successors cannot reproduce experiments. Open-source ELN eLabFTW has 266 open issues, with a cluster (Oct 2026) about team export/import losing groups, permissions, signatures and timestamps when migrating instances
failure_frequency: unknown; the paper-notebook default is described as the norm for academic/government labs (older sources, 2009-2019)
cost_of_failure: unknown in dollars; reproducibility loss and repeated re-optimization of protocols by successors
existing_workaround: Paper + scanned PDFs on shared drives; tablet-based ELNs for individuals; Google Docs; institutional ELN mandates; eLabFTW self-hosting
who_pays_today: Institutions paying LabArchives/Benchling/eLabFTW site licenses; labs paying in lost time; IT staff hosting open-source ELNs

sources.note: Review noting most academic and government labs continue to use paper notebooks despite ELN advantages.

'Make it better but don't change anything': study of ELN adoption resistance; the 169-respondent barrier survey surfaced in search synthesis may be from this or a related paper (attribution unverified).
Grad student describes undergrads writing on paper and uploading scans, and bench-side friction with computers.
UW-Madison campus-wide ELN rollout after pilots; shows adoption works when institution-led.
266 open issues on the leading open-source ELN; Oct 2026 cluster on lossy team export/import and attachment/filter bugs indicates migration friction.

firsthand_evidence: A graduate student blogger (2019) wrote that undergrads in their lab keep paper notebooks and upload scans to a shared drive, and that a tablet ELN is their own preferred option; eLabFTW users in October 2026 filed a dozen issues about data (groups, permissions, signatures, revisions) being lost on team export/import.
key_unknowns: Current 2026 ELN penetration in US academic labs (no recent survey found); whether the gap is tooling or incentives; whether PIs will pay for anything beyond free tiers of LabArchives/Benchling.
technical_unlock: Voice/photo capture at the bench with LLM transcription into structured protocol steps could remove the bench-side friction that keeps paper in use; this is the one angle not covered by incumbent ELNs, but it is close to the deprioritized 'LLM wrapper' category.
why_now: Reproducibility pressure and the NIH DMS policy (SCI-08) now require data provenance; multimodal LLMs make bench capture cheap for the first time.
existing_solutions: LabArchives, Benchling, eLabFTW (AGPL, 1.5k stars), SciNote, Labguru, RSpace, protocols.io for protocol sharing, labflow-eln (local-first, 2026)

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: Systematic-review title/abstract screening still takes months of manual work, and AI screening tools are hard to install, import into and trust
affected_user: Systematic reviewers and guideline developers (clinicians, nurses, epidemiologists, librarians), often small teams with no software support
job_to_be_done: Screen thousands of retrieved records down to the relevant set with near-perfect recall, and document the process for PRISMA
current_process: Export records from PubMed/Scopus/Embase, deduplicate, dual-screen manually in Rayyan/Covidence/Excel; increasingly try active-learning tools (ASReview) or LLM screeners (MetaScreener, 1.3k stars)
what_fails: Manual screening consumes months; LLM screeners cut person-hours by roughly two-thirds to three-quarters (Review Copilot validation) but leave a median false-negative rate of ~4.6% (medRxiv, May 2026), which reviewers cannot accept for recall-critical reviews; no LLM method has reached perfect recall while meaningfully reducing load (MechaScreener authors). ASReview users report RIS imports failing, records failing to load, lost labeling tags, projects not upgrading, and inability to resume on a new computer after a crash (2026 issues)
failure_frequency: Per review: every systematic review; the ASReview tracker shows a steady stream of import/load failures through 2026 (94 open issues)
cost_of_failure: Months of reviewer time per review (an automated case study completed a review in two weeks vs. typical multi-month timelines); unknown in dollars
existing_workaround: Dual human screening; hybrid co-screening (one human + model); accepting some recall loss; using commercial Covidence/Rayyan with institutional subscriptions
who_pays_today: Institutions subscribing to Covidence/DistillerSR/Rayyan; funders of guideline bodies; reviewers' own time

sources.note: GPT-4o mini title/abstract screening evaluation; reports a median false-negative rate of ~4.6% as a caveat.
MechaScreener tested on 15 reviews; notes no prior LLM method reliably reaches perfect recall while reducing load.
Meta-analysis of LLM screening performance; positions tools as assistants, not replacements.
Review Copilot validation: AI-assisted screening took roughly two-thirds to three-quarters fewer person-hours.
94 open issues; 2026 reports of RIS import failures, records failing to load, lost tags, failed upgrades, inability to resume after crash.
MetaScreener (1.3k stars), meta-pipe, citationchaser and others show a crowded tooling space focused on screening/retrieval.

firsthand_evidence: ASReview users in 2026 filed issues that new records fail to load on asreview.app, that RIS files cannot be imported into an existing project on Mac, that labeling tags vanish when a comment is added, and that a project could not be resumed on a new computer after a crash (paraphrased from issue titles).
key_unknowns: How many reviews are started per year by teams without Covidence access; whether reviewers will pay individually; whether journals/guideline bodies will accept LLM-assisted single screening; actual reviewer-hours per review in 2026.
technical_unlock: Cheap LLM screening with calibrated recall thresholds plus a workflow that preserves PRISMA audit trails; the technical pieces exist, the gap is reliability of import/dedup/resume and trust in recall.
why_now: 2026 saw a wave of preprints validating LLM screening and the first large open-source LLM screeners; reviewers are now choosing tools rather than asking whether to automate.
existing_solutions: Covidence, Rayyan, DistillerSR, EPPI-Reviewer, ASReview (open source), MetaScreener, meta-pipe, CoLRev, Review Copilot

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: Scientific analysis packages go unmaintained when the single grad student or postdoc who wrote them leaves, breaking downstream pipelines
affected_user: Bioinformaticians and computational scientists who depend on niche R/Python packages (e.g., flow/mass cytometry preprocessing, LIMS), and the lone maintainers themselves
job_to_be_done: Run a published analysis pipeline today on current language/OS versions, and keep lab tooling working after its author graduates
current_process: Depend on packages published alongside papers; when they break, fork and patch locally, pin ancient environments, or rewrite; maintainers volunteer unpaid time until burnout
what_fails: Packages stop receiving updates: on the GitHub flow-cytometry topic, ParkerICI's premessa/panorama/vite/grappolo (FCS preprocessing/visualization) last updated 2021-2023; pytometry_legacy 2022; open-source LIMS baobab.lims and MetaLIMS last updated 2022. Tidelift's 2024 survey (via secondary) found 60% of maintainers had quit or considered quitting; a 2026 preprint (BurnRiSc) argues a lone maintainer's departure can break infrastructure many systems depend on. A 2025 counter-study argues scientific OSS is abandoned less often than assumed, so the rate is contested.
failure_frequency: unknown; contested between the 'abandonment' narrative and arXiv 2504.18971's counterpoint
cost_of_failure: unknown in dollars; time spent re-implementing or pinning environments; irreproducible published analyses
existing_workaround: Forking, Docker/conda pinning, Bioconductor's enforced build checks, migrating to actively maintained alternatives (FlowKit/FlowIO), institutional RSE groups where they exist
who_pays_today: Funders via RSE positions (CZI EOSS, NSF POSE), institutions with research software engineering groups, and mostly unpaid maintainers

sources.note: BurnRiSc preprint: maintainer burnout as a sustainability problem; lone-departure risk; cites surveys showing burnout is widespread.
IEEE CiSE paper proposing quality metrics for scientific OSS sustainability, framed around reproducibility.
Counterpoint: scientific OSS is less likely to be abandoned than assumed (title only seen).
'People First' talk: research software sustainability depends on maintainer wellbeing; names burnout and institutional precarity.
Secondary summary of Tidelift 2024 survey: 60% of maintainers quit or considered quitting; median one active maintainer for top packages.
Of 20 top repos, at least 6 (ParkerICI premessa/panorama/grappolo, pytometry_legacy, etc.) have had no update since 2021-2023.
Open-source LIMS baobab.lims, MetaLIMS and parkour last updated 2022; limbus 2024.

firsthand_evidence: No individual maintainer complaint captured; the Zenodo 'People First' talk and BurnRiSc preprint summarize community surveys reporting widespread burnout (paraphrased).
key_unknowns: Which packages are truly load-bearing vs. dead-on-arrival paper code; whether labs would pay for maintenance-as-a-service; whether AI-assisted porting (e.g., R-to-Python or dependency bumps) is reliable enough for scientific correctness.
technical_unlock: LLM coding agents can now triage dependency breakage and generate patches for small scientific packages at low cost; combined with GitHub Actions, a 'keep this package building' service is technically feasible for a solo developer, though validation of scientific correctness remains hard.
why_now: Funding cuts (SCI-02) reduce RSE positions; AI-generated low-effort PRs add triage load (CodersCops blog); coding agents make maintenance cheaper for the first time.
existing_solutions: Bioconductor build system, rOpenSci peer review, Tidelift (commercial, enterprise-focused), CZI EOSS grants, Software Sustainability Institute, Research Software Alliance

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: Clinical trial sites lose most prospective participants before screening and eConsent adoption remains low despite perceived usefulness
affected_user: Clinical research coordinators and site managers at academic and community trial sites; sponsors and CROs paying for under-enrolling sites
job_to_be_done: Identify, contact, consent and enroll eligible participants fast enough to meet sponsor timelines
current_process: Manual EHR chart review, phone outreach, paper consent forms signed in person; some sites use eConsent platforms when sponsor-provided
what_fails: 80-86% of trials miss enrollment timelines (Tufts CSDD, cited via secondary sources); ~70% of sites miss projected targets and nearly 30% enroll no patients (secondary); 59% of sites report losing eligible patients due to inefficiencies in their own recruitment process (FierceBiotech survey via Clinical Trial Vanguard). eConsent adoption is often claimed at 50-75% but ACRP (Aug 2026) notes anecdotal evidence those numbers are inflated; a CRF Health survey of 105 site respondents found only 33% using or planning eConsent while 85% thought it useful
failure_frequency: Per trial: 80-86% of trials miss enrollment timelines (Tufts CSDD figure, date unverified)
cost_of_failure: unknown in verified dollars; trial delays are the main cost driver cited by vendors
existing_workaround: Sponsor-funded recruitment vendors, adding more sites, extending timelines, paper consent
who_pays_today: Sponsors and CROs (recruitment vendors, eConsent platforms such as Medidata/Veeva/Advarra), sites in coordinator time

sources.note: ACRP: eConsent adoption claims of 50-75% may be inflated; sites report operational impacts.
CRF Health survey of 105 site respondents: 33% using/planning eConsent, 85% believe it useful.
59% of sites losing eligible patients before screening due to recruitment inefficiencies (survey reported by FierceBiotech).
Vendor blog aggregating Tufts CSDD 80-86% timeline-miss statistic; secondary and unverified.

firsthand_evidence: None captured; all sources are industry surveys or vendor aggregations.
key_unknowns: Primary Tufts/WCG data behind the recruitment figures; what blocks site-level eConsent (cost, IRB, sponsor mandates, 21 CFR Part 11 validation); whether a non-institutional founder can sell to sites at all given HIPAA/Part 11 requirements.
technical_unlock: none obvious for a solo founder without institutional access; regulated (Part 11, HIPAA) and sponsor-driven purchasing make an MVP hard
why_now: ACRP's 2026 series signals sites are now being measured on eConsent operational impact; FDA decentralized-trial guidance (not verified in this search) encourages remote consent
existing_solutions: Medidata eConsent, Veeva, Advarra, Florence eConsent, DocuSign-based workflows; recruitment vendors (Trialfacts, Antidote, ClinOne)

domain: Scientific discovery and accessible research tools
title: NIH Data Management and Sharing policy compliance adds administrative load without producing the data sharing it was meant to
affected_user: NIH-funded PIs and their lab staff; central research-administration and library data-services staff at institutions
job_to_be_done: Write a compliant DMS plan for every NIH proposal, then actually deposit data in an appropriate repository with correct metadata by award end
current_process: PIs draft plans from library templates (Stanford, Duke, Columbia, Drexel guides); institutions staff data librarians; NIH introduced a new shorter standardized DMS format effective May 25, 2026 (NOT-OD-26-046) explicitly to reduce burden
what_fails: COGR projected (2022, 34 institutions) >$500K/yr central admin cost plus a similar amount at the academic level for mid/large institutions, and warned researchers would shift from lab work to admin tasks; FDP pilot noted significant variation in institute-specific requirements creates substantial burden before drafting; a Johns Hopkins survey of 50 NIH-funded researchers found data sharing and utilization have not increased and investigators hold a negative stigma toward the policy
failure_frequency: Every NIH application (policy effective Jan 2023); per-institution cost projections above
cost_of_failure: COGR projection: >$500K/yr central plus similar academic-level cost per mid/large institution (forecast, not measured); researcher time unmeasured
existing_workaround: Library template plans, DMPTool, boilerplate copied between proposals, minimal deposits to generalist repositories
who_pays_today: Institutions (data librarians, research admin), PIs' time, NIH (budget line items for data management allowed in awards)

sources.note: COGR survey of 34 institutions projecting >$500K/yr central cost plus similar academic-level cost.
COGR cost-of-compliance document.
JHU study: survey of 50 NIH-funded researchers found no increase in data sharing/utilization and negative stigma toward the policy (small sample).
FDP pilot: institute-specific requirement variation places substantial burden on researchers.
Duke guide: new shorter standardized DMS format required from May 25, 2026 (NOT-OD-26-046), designed to reduce burden.

firsthand_evidence: JHU survey respondents (50 NIH-funded researchers) expressed a negative stigma toward the policy and reported no increase in data sharing (paraphrased from abstract summary).
key_unknowns: No post-implementation (2024-2026) burden measurement was found; whether NIH's May 2026 format change materially reduces time; whether institutions would buy tooling beyond DMPTool.
technical_unlock: LLM drafting of plans is already commoditized (and is the deprioritized 'wrapper' pattern); the harder unmet piece is automated repository deposit with metadata from lab data, which requires integration with ELNs/instruments (see SCI-03/SCI-04).
why_now: NIH changed the DMS format in May 2026, an explicit admission of burden; funding cuts reduce admin staff available to help.
existing_solutions: DMPTool, DMPonline, library consult services, Figshare/Dryad/Zenodo deposit, Dataverse
